cells.tense: The pull toward what you want is lit by work you have already done.
cells.act: see how it works underneath, apart from this instance
cells.ask: Take something you're after right now. Look at how it actually works underneath — not this one shot, the machinery. Say that in a line before you plan anything else.
cells.core:
The draw you feel toward what you want isn't wishful. It sits on work already done, and because of that you can move toward goals without forcing each step. Direction through resistance, and the resistance doesn't eat you. What you're pointed at holds still enough to head toward honestly, and people can tell it isn't performance.

What serves you now is seeing the machinery, not adding to the plan. Underneath whatever you're currently after, there's a way it works — the same shape showing up in how you choose, how you recover, how you know when a thing is real. Once you can say that shape in a line, you'll be able to tell which new thing belongs to it and which is only loud. That's how a direction stays a direction instead of turning into a run of bright impulses.

cells.verb: to head toward what you can see

cells.tense: The light is being aimed so far past the present that today's work stands in its shadow.
cells.act: wait until you know which part matters, then begin with that part
cells.ask: Before you start the next big thing, hold off until one piece plainly counts more than the others. Do only that piece today. The rest can stay dark till tomorrow.
cells.core:
You have the light pointed down the road so far that it's dazzling you instead of showing you the road. Every plan is for a version of you who hasn't shown up, and the plans keep getting brighter while the actual days get smaller. The pull is real. It's just running out past the hands that have to do the work, and the brightness is starting to feel like pressure.

The move is scale, not effort. Before you begin, wait until one piece plainly counts more than the others, and start there — the other parts can stay dark for now. Once the light sits on the next hour instead of the next year, it's useful again. You'll still be heading for the same destination. You'll just be able to see where your feet go and whether a step counted.

cells.tense: You once headed somewhere, and what remains is the memory of heading there.
cells.act: keep showing up to it without forcing a result
cells.ask: Choose something you used to care about. Be there for it this week, ten minutes a day, and force nothing — no outcome, no sign it's taking. Just show up.
cells.core:
Where you head toward what you want, the direction has gone quiet. You still know how to point at something, but nothing you were moving toward is in view, and you've stopped expecting that to change. That isn't laziness. It's what unflowered work does — the hands stay trained, the ability to want is what's tired, and the tiredness is not a character flaw.

What's left isn't nothing. Something in you still knows how to show up for a thing, so show up for one, small, and demand nothing back. Smaller than feels serious. No progress report, no checking whether it's taking. Care that asks for nothing is how a starved thing gets fed, and you don't have to point it anywhere yet. Keep showing up. Let direction come back in its time, or not yet.

cells.tense: You are already the thing you keep waiting for permission to be.
cells.act: keep it at its real size when you are asked to shrink it
cells.ask: Someone will ask what you're after, and your reflex will be a small answer. Don't make it smaller this time. Say it at the size it actually is, once.
cells.core:
You have a pull toward something, and it's been steering your choices for a while — you just don't count it as one. When people ask what you're after, you make it smaller on the way out, and that smaller answer is what you hear yourself saying. The heading is happening. You file it under staying busy.

What you've built is bigger than the story you tell about it, and the gap costs you: nobody can help you with a goal you've filed as a habit. Try saying it at full size the next time someone asks, for one sentence, and stop there. You don't need a speech or a defense. A thing said at its true size starts getting answered, and the first answer is usually a person who can already see it.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person's reaching is genuinely theirs and lighting anything real — the record supports orientation and pull, not its correctness or that a given goal is worth it. Reader objection: 'I'm not shiny or stuck, I'm just tired of chasing things that didn't land.' The ask survives being wrong: naming the pattern across attempts teaches something either way and asks nothing of the goals themselves. Sentence serving the writer more than the person: any line implying their light was already obvious to everyone around them — cut. Also checked: Too Much and Too Little as opposite failures of the same capacity — projecting the light ahead of the work versus the light having gone out of the work.

attempts.check: The record supports a pull toward something desired and momentum toward it, not that the goal is reachable or that the shine is visible to others — every cell now stays with orientation and direction and drops any claim about outcomes or how it looks from outside. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not glowing and not lost, I'm just going.' The asks survive that: tracing how a thing worked before, starting with the part that matters, doing something small while asking nothing, and not shrinking a want all teach something even if the read is wrong about them. The sentence that served the writer more than the person was any line implying others already see their light — cut. Too Much and Too Little read as one capacity failing forward and failing quiet: aiming the light past the work, versus the light having gone out of the work.
